item.title: GSK is two shots away from clean bill of health
item.description: One of Europe’s most cheaply valued drugmakers, the £75 bln group run by Luke Miels is turning a corner. Fears over expiring patents are easing thanks to a booming oncology unit. A £40 bln sales target looks hard, but Miels may fix that with canny dealmaking and luck in the lab.
item.dc:creator: Aimee Donnellan
item.content:encoded: If GSK (GSK.L) were a patient doctors would be starting to hope that it’s on the mend. Despite being one of the cheapest of the global pharma stocks, new CEO Luke Miels is ploughing money into research and development and doing savvy deals. The big question is can he deliver on his target of over £40 billion in sales by 2031 . Signs of a recovery have appeared slowly. When Miels’ predecessor Emma Walmsley was in charge, she spun out the consumer goods business which makes Sensodyne toothpaste, now called Haleon (HLN.L) . Investors hoped the surgery would unleash a leaner, less indebted business that could focus its efforts on dealmaking and its core areas of vaccines, HIV and general medicines including inhalers and antibiotics. So far, that's yet to translate into a material valuation bump: GSK trades at around 10 times forward earnings, in line with its multiple when Haleon was spun off in 2022 , and below peers like AstraZeneca (AZN.L) , Novartis (NOVN.S) and Roche (ROPC.S) . The main reason is fear of what comes next. Dolutegravir, GSK’s star HIV treatment which accounted for 17% of GSK’s near £33 billion of sales last year, loses patent protection in the US from 2028. Analysts polled by Visible Alpha expect revenue in that division to halve by 2031. Vaccines have also lost steam. Anti vaccine sentiment is growing in the US, and analysts expect the division to grow sales by an average of less than 2% over the next five years. However, Miels is plugging these holes partly by bolstering the group’s growing cancer business. Last year, sales in oncology rose by over 40% to nearly £2 billion and they are expected to reach over £5 billion pounds by 2031. And he’s hoping to boost that further through deals and in-house drug development. In June, he splurged [USN:L6N42H0KM TEXT:"$11 billion"] on US lung cancer specialist Nuvalent. The business won regulatory approval for one of its drugs a month after the deal was announced and GSK is expecting to hear about another remedy later this year. This week GSK won regulatory backing for a new rectal cancer drug. Growth in GSK’s oncology business should help offset the decline in HIV as dolutegravir's patents expire. The cancer success isn't the only sign that GSK's plan to boost in-house drug development is paying off. Miels is expecting to start over 20 new late stage drug trials this year. Potential blockbuster drugs include a hepatitis B remedy bepirovirsen which it reckons will generate £2 billion in annual sales. Berenberg analysts estimate the group's likely return on research investment is now over 10%, healthily exceeding the sector's 8% cost of capital. GSK is still some way off hitting Miels' target to reach £40 billion of sales by 2031. But the gap is closing: Analysts polled by Visible Alpha estimate sales of £37 billion that year, up from less than £34 billion a year ago. To hit the magic number, Miels will probably need to do more small deals, as well as keep securing fresh drug approvals. But the danger that he will resort to more large risky takeovers is probably easing. That, along with GSK's broader turnaround, means its valuation should start to catch up with its healthier peers. Follow Aimee Donnellan on LinkedIn . GSK will unveil its third quarter earnings on October 28. The US Food and Drug Administration on October 19 approved GSK’s Jemperli, an immunotherapy for locally advanced rectal cancer. CONTEXT-NEWS

item.title: Nigeria reports Ebola case as outbreak reaches West Africa
item.description: Nigeria reported its first Ebola case in more than a decade on Tuesday, becoming the fourth African country and the most populous yet to be affected by an outbreak that health officials have described as the fastest-spreading on record.
item.dc:creator: Elisha Bala-Gbogbo, Camillus Eboh
item.content:encoded: Nigeria reported its first Ebola case in more than a decade on Tuesday, becoming the fourth African country and the most populous yet to be affected by an outbreak that health officials have described as the [USN:L6N4421DF TEXT:"fastest-spreading on record"]. The Ebola species behind the outbreak kills about half of those infected and has no approved treatment or vaccine. Since the first cases were confirmed in Democratic Republic of Congo in May, the disease has killed 4,646 people. Health officials fear misinformation and [USN:L8N45M12L TEXT:"funding shortfalls"] could fuel further spread within the region and across borders. Cases have also been reported in Uganda and, more recently, Kenya. "Ebola is now affecting three regions of Africa. The situation demands urgent action and political leadership at the highest level," Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Director General Jean Kaseya said on X on Wednesday. The Nigerian case involves a Ugandan woman who arrived in Nigeria's capital Abuja via Addis Ababa on October 5, Odianosen Ehiakhamen of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control told Arise TV on Tuesday. She began feeling unwell two days later and sought treatment at a private hospital in Abuja on October 11 with malaria-like symptoms, but her condition did not improve, Ehiakhamen said. CONCERN OF 'PAN-AFRICAN EVENT' After health officials learned she had recently travelled to Uganda, one of the countries affected by the current outbreak, they tested her for Ebola on October 19. The positive result was confirmed on Tuesday. "My concern, now that this has spread from East Africa to West Africa, is that we now have a pan-African event, as opposed to a few at-risk countries," said Ayoade Alakija, a Nigerian physician who co-chairs a G7 committee for investment in global health. Alakija also noted that it had taken 12 days since the woman fell sick for her to be tested for Ebola, potentially exposing many other people to the infection. "Abuja is one of Africa's main cities ... with air and road connections daily, multiple, across the world. It’s a very different prospect – and that's what worries me — the amount of time it took." Nigerian authorities have identified 44 contacts, most of them healthcare workers. They include the patient's husband, a Swiss national who lives with her in Abuja. Officials are also tracing passengers who travelled with her from Uganda to Nigeria but do not believe she was symptomatic during the flight. Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate told public broadcaster NTA that the woman was in isolation and receiving treatment. UGANDA SAYS IT HAS NO ACTIVE EBOLA CASES Uganda's health ministry said the woman had travelled to Congo, where more than 9,500 Ebola cases have been recorded across eight provinces. It was not immediately clear where she had been in Congo, and Nigerian authorities have not confirmed that she had visited the country. "Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here," Uganda's health ministry said, adding that the country has no active Ebola cases. Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country [USN:L6N44N0VL TEXT:"Ebola-free"] in August. Earlier this month, Kenya reported its first Ebola case, involving a traveller who arrived from Congo via Uganda. The country has since reported [USN:L1N4660OP TEXT:"nine cases"], all linked to the same patient. The spread of Ebola to Kenya raised questions about the effectiveness of [USN:L6N45S157 TEXT:"border screening systems"] designed to prevent cross-border transmission. Pate, Nigeria's health minister, said the country had successfully contained Ebola in 2014 during the West African epidemic, the largest outbreak on record. He said Nigeria had the systems in place to respond to the new case.

item.title: Nasdaq leads Wall Street gains as SpaceX, Super Micro boost AI sentiment
item.description: The tech-heavy Nasdaq led Wall Street to a higher close on Wednesday after quarterly results from SpaceX and Super Micro Computer improved investor appetite for artificial intelligence-related stocks while weakness in communication services stocks capped gains.
item.dc:creator: Sinead Carew, Purvi Agarwal
item.content:encoded: The tech-heavy Nasdaq led Wall Street to a higher close on Wednesday after quarterly results from SpaceX and Super Micro Computer improved investor appetite for artificial intelligence-related stocks while weakness in communication services stocks capped gains. SpaceX shares (SPCX.O) finished up 7.8% after Elon Musk's rocket and space technology firm posted its first profit as a public company. Musk said, following the report, that [USN:L4N4661M0 TEXT:"a merger of SpaceX"] and Tesla (TSLA.O) would be "a good idea," also boosting Tesla shares. Elsewhere in earnings, Super Micro (SMCI.O) shares jumped 9.6% and it was among the S&P 500's top gainers after the AI server maker [USN:L4N4661QH TEXT:"forecast"] quarterly revenue and profit margin above Wall Street estimates, signaling that AI demand remained resilient. The report also benefited peers HPE (HPE.N) , which rose 3.7%, and Dell (DELL.N) , which rose 5.3%. The reports provided some reassurance to investors who have been worried about the sustainability of massive spending on AI buildouts and their profitability. The technology sector was hammered last week by a selloff in AI-linked stocks, with data center operator CoreWeave (CRWV.O) at the center of the storm. The SpaceX news "pushes back on some of the investor worries" about AI along with some help from Super Micro, according to Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones. Kourkafas said the reports will not "answer all the questions investors have on returns on AI investments, but it's a good start." As a result, the S&P 500 Information Technology index (.SPLRCT) finished up 1.6%, the biggest gainer among the S&P 500's 11 major industry sectors. "It's really a positive technology story for almost anyone that is somewhat involved in the artificial intelligence ecosystem," said Marc Dizard, chief investment officer at Huntington Bank. "The technology market reaction has been a reaffirmation that the artificial intelligence trade is still intact," he added. However, Dizard said sentiment can quickly shift around AI and that investors will seek reaffirmation when they monitor earnings reports from other companies. Shares in [USN:L4N4671S3 TEXT:"Meta"] (META.O) rose 3% in late trading after it released its quarterly results following the regular session's close. After finishing up 3.4% in the regular session, [USN:L4N4671SD TEXT:"Tesla"] shares rose another 1.6% following its report, which was also issued after the close. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 360.21 points, or 0.69%, to 52,856.09, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 44.60 points, or 0.58%, to 7,757.17 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) gained 278.04 points, or 1.05%, to 26,702.86. Within technology, one of the strongest areas was chips with a 2% rally in the Philadelphia Semiconductor index (.SOX) , which has had a volatile month so far including an eight-session selloff. Gains in the benchmark S&P 500 were limited however by a 1.3% decline in communication services stocks (.SPLRCL) . The biggest losers included telecom operators such as AT&T (T.N) , which sank 6.5% even as it beat [USN:L4N4670UN TEXT:"third-quarter"] revenue and profit expectations. The SpaceX results, along with a recent wireless spectrum purchase, fanned fears that it could become a formidable competitor in telecoms, according to Dizard. T-Mobile US (TMUS.O) shares fell 2.5% and Verizon Communications (VZ.N) lost 2.2%. Also in communications services, Netflix (NFLX.O) shares sank 5.3% after the video streaming company issued [USN:L6N4661BU TEXT:"a weaker-than-expected forecast"] for its fourth-quarter profit. Google's parent Alphabet (GOOGL.O) also declined 1.6%. Abbott Laboratories (ABT.N) shares dropped 1.9% after the medical device maker cut its [USN:L4N4670ZJ TEXT:"2026 sales growth forecast"]. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.37-to-1 ratio on the NYSE where there were 131 new highs and 221 new lows. On the Nasdaq, 2,690 stocks rose and 2,068 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.3-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 26 new 52-week highs and 3 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 53 new highs and 216 new lows. On US exchanges roughly 16.11 billion shares changed hands compared with the 17.10 billion average for the last 20 sessions.

item.title: Anthropic, music publishers square off on 'fair use' defense in AI copyright case
item.description: Anthropic urged a judge in California on Wednesday to rule that the AI company's use of millions of song lyrics to train its chatbot Claude is protected as "fair use" under US copyright law, as it seeks to scuttle a lawsuit brought by Universal Music Group and other music publishers.
item.dc:creator: Blake Brittain
item.content:encoded: Anthropic urged a judge in California on Wednesday to rule that the AI company's use of millions of song lyrics to train its chatbot Claude is protected as "fair use" under US copyright law, as it seeks to scuttle a lawsuit brought by Universal Music Group (UMG.AS) and other music publishers. US District Judge Eumi Lee did not rule at a hearing in San Jose but pressed both sides on the fair use question, which could be key to dozens of other high-stakes copyright infringement cases in the AI era. Lee also questioned the publishers' assertion that Claude's ability to compose lyrics threatens the market for the publishers' lyrics. Anthropic lawyer Sonal Mehta of WilmerHale argued that its AI training leads to the creation of transformative new content, putting it squarely under the fair use doctrine. The publishers' attorney Matt Oppenheim of Oppenheim + Zebrak responded that Anthropic misuses its lyrics to generate competing content that harms human songwriters. Oppenheim said Claude received nearly 120,000 requests to generate "synthetic" lyrics over a six-month period. He said large language models like Claude "could overwhelm the market with AI-generated content very easily." Mehta countered that AI has not reduced demand for the lyrics, and that the publishers could not identify any specific instances of market harm from Claude or other large language models. Mehta also said that UMG itself has said that AI is "overwhelmingly a net positive" for the music industry. EARLY FAIR USE RULINGS Fair use could determine the fate of pending lawsuits brought by authors, news outlets, visual artists and others against tech giants including Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta Platforms over their AI training. Two other Northern California judges who have already weighed in on the closely watched issue have split on whether generative AI training generally makes fair use of copyrighted material, which would shield tech companies from liability for using millions of copyrighted works to train their systems without content owners' permission. Now-retired US District Judge William Alsup sided with [USN:L6N3S50SQ TEXT:"Anthropic"] last year on its argument that its AI training made fair use of books. Two days later, US District Judge Vince Chhabria [USN:L6N3S10OC TEXT:"ruled for Meta"] in a similar lawsuit but warned that AI training “in many circumstances” would not be fair use. In the case being heard by Lee, music publishers UMG, Concord and ABKCO [USN:L1N3BO1X6 TEXT:"sued Anthropic"] in 2023, alleging its use of their lyrics to train Claude to respond to human prompts infringed their copyrights in hundreds of songs by artists including Beyonce, the Rolling Stones and the Beach Boys. Anthropic [USN:L6N41418J TEXT:"has argued"] that its AI training makes transformative use of song lyrics to "help Claude understand human language and enable progress and productivity in science, business and education."

item.title: Trump says fraud investigations make 'very big dent' in overseas scams
item.description: President Donald Trump said on Wednesday his administration has made a "very big dent" in scams by foreign criminal networks that lure Americans into fraudulent investments, focusing on an anti-fraud message ahead of November's midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Courtney Rozen
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump said on Wednesday his administration has made a "very big dent" in scams by foreign criminal networks that lure Americans into fraudulent investments, focusing on an anti-fraud message ahead of November's [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm elections"]. Trump, members of his cabinet and other top administration officials met at the White House for an event on cybercrime prevention, where FBI Director Kash Patel said his agency had taken down 20 scam compounds throughout the world. Early voting has already begun in many states ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, where Trump's Republican Party risks losing control of Congress while polls show that voters' top concern is the rising [USN:L6N44S0Y9 TEXT:"cost of living"]. "Federal law enforcement has been able to warn over 10,000 Americans targeted for victimization, and we've prevented $1.6 billion in losses — at least — this year," Trump said at the event. Americans filed more than 1 million complaints with the FBI about internet scams last year, a 17% increase from 2024, according to an FBI report. Cabinet officials at the meeting included Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth and Attorney General Todd Blanche, while White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller were also present. The president's team highlighted work to crack down on overseas crypto scams, with Miller saying that Trump "effectively declared cyber warfare against the cyber criminals." Trump's family has been heavily involved in soliciting investments in crypto . A Reuters investigation found the Republican president and his sons have added at least $2.3 billion to the family fortune from their main crypto ventures, while the investors they have wooed have taken a $2.3 billion hit. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly, in a statement to Reuters about its investigation, said: "All actions by President Trump and his administration are taken in the best interest of the American people." Trump in October 2025 [USN:FWN3W42W4 TEXT:"pardoned"] Changpeng Zhao, the convicted founder of the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Zhao quit his job after the [USN:L1N3CM1MQ TEXT:"company"] pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program. In a March executive order, Trump directed the Justice Department to prioritize identifying and prosecuting scammers who carry out crimes online. Trump later directed the Department of Homeland Security to [USN:FWN4491P7 TEXT:"work"] with private companies to surveil foreign criminal hacking groups.

item.title: Booking.com targeted in EU investigation into phishing scams, fraudulent listings
item.description: EU tech regulators will investigate whether online hotel reservation website Booking.com is doing enough to weed out fraudulent listings and phishing scams to comply with EU online content rules, the European Commission said on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Yun Chee Foo
item.content:encoded: EU tech regulators will investigate whether online hotel reservation website Booking.com is doing enough to weed out fraudulent listings and phishing scams to comply with EU online content rules, the European Commission said on Wednesday. The Commission, which is the EU tech and competition enforcer, said it opened an investigation following a preliminary probe and after analysing risk assessment reports submitted by Booking.com this year and the previous three years. Big online platforms are required to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content on their sites under the bloc's Digital Services Act, or risk fines of as much as 6% of their global annual turnover for violations. Booking.com said it was engaging constructively with the Commission. "Security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities at Booking.com," a spokesperson for the company said. "We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud, and protect travelers and partners." The EU investigation will focus on fake listings — such as for non-existent properties — impersonation fraud and non-compliant accommodation offers, and whether Booking.com has properly identified, assessed and mitigated the systemic risks related to these. Regulators will also look into phishing scams exploiting Booking.com's reservation and guest data shared with accommodation providers, the Commission said. A third element will be paid-for boosted listings not clearly identifiable as advertisements. Booking.com is part of Booking Holdings (BKNG.O) . "Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement. "The Digital Services Act sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously," she said.

item.title: Who is Stephen Hubbard, the US citizen released by Russia?
item.description: Here are details of Hubbard's case.
item.dc:creator: Lucy Papachristou
item.content:encoded: President Vladimir Putin announced the release of American citizen Stephen Hubbard from Russian detention on Wednesday, [USN:L6N4670LA TEXT:"at the start of talks"] with US special envoy Steve Witkoff. Here are details of Hubbard's case: WHO IS STEPHEN HUBBARD? Hubbard, 74, a retired schoolteacher, grew up in Big Rapids, Michigan, and served in the US Air Force and National Guard, according to military records cited by the New York Times. He earned a master’s degree in English and lived in Japan for 25 years where he taught English before moving to Cyprus and then, in 2014, to Izyum in eastern Ukraine with a Ukrainian partner, according to his sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox. Fox told Reuters in 2024 that Hubbard subsisted on a pension of about $300 a month and had few connections with local people. The siblings last spoke in September 2021. HOW WAS HE CAPTURED? Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022 and captured Izyum two months later. Ukrainian forces retook the city in September 2022, but Hubbard was already in Russian custody by then. Russian state media said Hubbard had been detained in April 2022 and alleged he had been manning a Ukrainian military checkpoint. Reuters could not independently establish the circumstances of his capture. Fox said she recognised her brother in a YouTube video showing a man being questioned about his views on Putin and the war. Another video showed him with his hands bound, being struck with a sandal. Reuters could not verify when or where the videos were recorded. WHY WAS HE IMPRISONED? Following a closed trial, a Moscow court convicted Hubbard of being a mercenary in October 2024 and sentenced him to six years and 10 months in prison.Prosecutors said Hubbard had joined a Ukrainian territorial defence unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and was promised $1,000 a month. Russian state media said he had pleaded guilty to the charges he faced. Fox questioned the reported confession, however, saying Hubbard held pro-Russian views and was unlikely to have taken up arms in his seventies. Martin De Luca, his US-based lawyer, told Reuters in June 2025 that Hubbard had told him the charges against him were false and that he was not in any combat or military unit. He cited Hubbard as telling him Russian soldiers had simply grabbed him from his house. WHAT IS HUBBARD'S CURRENT STATUS? In January 2025, Washington designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained, enabling the US government to pursue negotiations for his release. The State Department has said Russia refused to grant US officials consular access. The New York Times reported in February 2025 that Hubbard had been moved through at least five Russian detention centres before his trial. His lawyer said Hubbard's legal team found out only in April 2025 that he was being held in a facility in the Mordovia region, east of Moscow.

item.title: Russia frees retired US schoolteacher in goodwill gesture as Putin meets Witkoff
item.description: Russia freed Stephen Hubbard, a retired US schoolteacher in custody since 2022, from prison on Wednesday and took him to St Petersburg to fly back to the United States, after talks that Washington said were a step toward ending the war in Ukraine.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia freed [USN:L8N4670PP TEXT:"Stephen Hubbard"], a retired US schoolteacher in custody since 2022, from prison on Wednesday and took him to St Petersburg to fly back to the United States, after talks that Washington said were a step toward ending the war in Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin made the announcement at a meeting in St Petersburg with US envoy Steve Witkoff, who later said the talks will continue toward planned technical-level discussions involving the US, Russia and Ukraine. Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" in thanking him for the move, a remark that drew sharp rebuke from Republican and Democratic lawmakers given Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The prisoner release comes as President Donald Trump's recent gestures toward Moscow, including a deal to buy Russian diesel and a waiver of new sanctions, have already sparked bipartisan pushback in the US Congress and worry in European capitals. Putin's spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, said Putin had freed Hubbard, 74, at Trump's request, and that he had also taken into account the American's poor health. Trump later confirmed he had asked Putin on a call in recent days, and Putin agreed. "The president sends his thanks, our whole nation sends their thanks, because of Stephen Hubbard," Witkoff told Putin in the meeting shown on Russian state TV. "Because of you he's going home to his family." In a video shared with Reuters, Hubbard, wearing a dark fleece and clean-shaven, is seen in an undisclosed location in Russia shaking Witkoff's hand and thanking him. Later, Trump posted a picture of Hubbard appearing inside a plane with others and holding an American flag. Hubbard's son, Joseph Coleman, told Reuters in a voice message that he spoke briefly by phone with his father before he boarded the airplane in Russia. "Today he seemed light in his step, a sense of happiness in his voice", Coleman said. THREE-WAY MEETING PLANNED ON WAR Witkoff called the talks with Putin "constructive" and said in a post on X that he had also met Ukrainian and European leaders in Oslo to advance Trump's mission to end the war. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he supported the US proposal for three-way talks with Russia and the United States at the level of negotiators to be held as soon as possible, preferably by early November. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere, who also met Witkoff, had earlier said the talks will likely happen in mid-November and focus on a potential post-conflict security structure. On Wednesday evening, officials in Kyiv said Russian forces attacked the capital city with ballistic missiles that damaged homes and a petrol station and caused injuries. 'HUMANITARIAN' Witkoff's praise for Putin over Hubbard's release was scorned by some in Washington. "Look up the definition of 'humanitarian.' What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say," Republican US Senator Thom Tillis said in an X post directed at the US envoy. Trump, asked about Witkoff's "humanitarian" comment, told reporters at the White House: “Well, I guess you have to say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man, who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life, out. But I wouldn't say anything one way or the other." The US "gave nothing in exchange" for the prisoner release, Trump said, adding "we're getting closer" to settling the war. "He is the happiest man around," Trump said of Hubbard. "This was very surprising to him, but I did it, it really took place on a phone call at the end of last week with President Putin, so we appreciate it very much. And his family is extremely happy." FAMILY, LAWYER DISPUTED CONVICTION Hubbard, a native of Michigan, had been serving a prison sentence of six years and 10 months in Russia following a conviction for mercenary activity in a closed-door trial. He was arrested in April 2022 in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izyum, where Russian prosecutors alleged he had been manning a Ukrainian military checkpoint. Prosecutors said Hubbard had joined a Ukrainian territorial defence unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and was promised $1,000 a month. Russian state media reported he pleaded guilty to the charges. But Hubbard's US-based lawyer, Martin De Luca, previously told Reuters that Hubbard had told him the charges against him were false and that he was not in any combat or military unit. In a 2024 interview with Reuters, Hubbard's sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, also disputed the idea that her brother took up arms for any government, calling him "so non-military" and pointing out his advanced age. De Luca on Wednesday thanked Trump, Witkoff and other US officials for securing the release, calling it "a dividend earned along the hard road to peace". As of Wednesday, Hubbard was the only US prisoner held by Russia who was designated by Washington as "wrongfully detained". The Trump administration secured the release last year of another American jailed in Russia, schoolteacher [USN:S0N3P202G TEXT:"Marc Fogel"], who had been serving a 14-year prison term for drug smuggling.

item.title: Putin agrees to resume 3-way peace talks with Ukraine and US
item.description: Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month, the Kremlin said on Wednesday, after Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War Two.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month, the Kremlin said on Wednesday, after Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War Two. The negotiations in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia - the release of [USN:L8N4670PP TEXT:"Stephen Hubbard, a retired US school teacher"] held in Russia whom US President Trump had asked the Kremlin chief to release. Wednesday's encounter unfolded amid concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the United States is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine's military communications. The latest talks also came more than two years since Trump promised in his successful election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours. The Kremlin said the new 3-way peace talks, which would be at a technical level, could take place in Abu Dhabi and would be focused on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended. They could begin sometime on or after November 10, it said. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran . The Kremlin was less upbeat, however, about the outcome of talks Witkoff had held a day earlier in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, the leaders of Finland and Norway, and European and NATO representatives. Witkoff told Putin the talks had been characterised by "some degree of momentum" and a US official said Ukraine had brought [USN:L1N466099 TEXT:"new ideas and proposals"]. "These nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us," Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the St Petersburg meeting - which lasted nearly three hours. POSSIBLE MEETING BETWEEN TRUMP, PUTIN AND XI Ukraine and Russia remain far apart when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal, though Trump has recently intensified pressure on Ukraine to strike some kind of a deal. He said on Tuesday it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face "a very bad thing." Putin also used Wednesday's talks to offer to help Trump deal with Iran, saying Russia had a decades-long relationship with Tehran which it has repeatedly offered to leverage to address US concerns about Iran's nuclear programme. Putin told Witkoff it was possible and necessary to get a deal with Tehran, the Kremlin said. Russia could also supply vast quantities of fertiliser to the United States to help US farmers, the Russian president told Witkoff. [USN:L1N4650BJ TEXT:"A potential meeting in China next month"] with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was also discussed. The Kremlin said Beijing was already preparing what it said would be the first meeting of its kind in history. 'NEW IDEAS' Putin has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims, which include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, no NATO membership for Kyiv, and an overall peace deal rather than a temporary ceasefire. Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special investment envoy, was also present at the talks with Witkoff and the Kremlin said that major joint economic projects had been discussed, including some that were close to being realised. Witkoff said he had brought some documents with him containing various ideas for a potential peace deal for Putin to review, and that Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, also wanted to convey some ideas to Putin. Kushner later joined the meeting remotely by phone. Zelenskiy said he [USN:L1N4670EW TEXT:"hoped to discuss key issues"] on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin and Trump. The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelenskiy meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared in advance by aides to make it worthwhile. FRAYING US-UKRAINE TIES US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month to help lower prices in the United States. High fuel costs since he launched strikes on Iran have hurt his Republicans ahead of November legislative elections. Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starshield military satellite system, though Zelenskiy said that Tuesday's Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those issues. Citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that billionaire Elon Musk had last week ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Musk has said any such decision is taken by the US military or the president. Trump has said he was not responsible and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated on Wednesday that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv's ability to access Starlink.

item.title: Government websites go dark after AI-discovered flaw sparks security scramble
item.description: Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Wednesday after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, Leo Marchandon, Kanjyik Ghosh, Rajveer Pardesi
item.content:encoded: Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Wednesday after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems. Developers of the PHP programming language on Wednesday released urgent new fixes to vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years until they were uncovered using AI, saying all users were "encouraged to update immediately." With tech firms warning that some hackers were already exploiting the flaws, government agencies across Europe were among those that took sites offline as a precaution. Because a fix is now public and artificial intelligence tools are able to reverse engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers jumped to get ahead of the updates. AI was powering a "race to exploit," said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He said the next step was the "mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the internet." PHP — a language that dates back to the early 1990s and initially stood for "Personal Home Page" — underpins huge parts of the public-facing web and is baked into WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, meaning any critical vulnerability potentially has enormous knock-on consequences. "All servers using any version of PHP released in the last 20 years will be vulnerable," said Tiffany Farriss, the interim chief executive of the Drupal Association. "This issue impacts the majority of the internet." Cybersecurity agencies around the world have urged PHP users to update immediately or take websites offline until patches can be applied. According to data from Censys, the internet intelligence firm, about 1.5 million out of 2.6 million hosts report running a version of PHP for which there is no fix. The Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities. The operator of the online encyclopedia Wikipedia also said it had taken down an unspecified number of systems until they could be safely patched, while the Internet Archive, the sprawling online library, said it also briefly went offline to deal with the issue. Even some world leaders weighed in. The Dutch prime minister said he was closely monitoring the situation. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in a post on X said website owners should "check whether your live site uses PHP and prepare to apply the new fix." BUG FOUND WITH AI The flaw in PHP was discovered using artificial intelligence, two cybersecurity companies said in independent reports. Calif said in a blog post it found the flaws with the help of a large language model on August 1 and had been working on a fix ever since. Alphabet-owned (GOOGL.O) cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post that it too had discovered it with the help of Wiz Atlas, its autonomous AI vulnerability research tool, as well as Google's Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. The vulnerabilities remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to take advantage of, Wiz's post said. "Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale," it said. "With AI, this is no longer a barrier." Calif and Wiz said they coordinated with one another and the PHP team and OpenAI on the discovery. In a statement, the White House said it was made aware of the flaw on Friday. In a blog post late on Wednesday, Amazon (AMZN.O) security chief CJ Moses said the tech giant's security team detected an attempt to exploit the vulnerabilities against one of its decoy "honeypot" systems on October 17, four days before public disclosure. The attempt on the system came from an anonymous internet address, suggesting the activity was conducted by a threat actor, Moses said, adding it was unclear how the actor learned of the flaws while they were under embargo. More attempts followed on Wednesday by multiple actors before the embargo lifted. Amazon said it was still unclear whether any of the attempts would have worked against real websites, adding the flaws were "now being broadly exploited in the wild." CRITICAL SOFTWARE PHP is a [USN:L6N467127 TEXT:"programming language"] used to run websites. When a visitor loads a page, a server running PHP assembles the content and sends it to the browser. It is free, open-source software maintained by volunteers. Its ubiquity — PHP runs roughly 75% of websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs — has made experts anxious. AI-assisted hacking campaigns, which have [USN:L6N46118G TEXT:"proliferated in recent weeks"], could wreak havoc on unpatched servers, said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at King's College London. "The scale is huge, and with AI, exploitation may happen instantly," Olejnik said. WordPress.com operator Automattic said users of its hosted solutions and Tumblr were safe from the bug . Risks were higher for small PHP-powered websites run by individuals or organizations with limited technical resources, often on shared hosting services where customers do not directly manage the underlying servers. MASS OUTAGES In the Netherlands, several organizations followed the example of the National Cyber Security Centre and took public-facing websites offline, including the Port of Rotterdam, government portal Overheid.nl, the national soccer association KNVB, the websites for the country's five largest political parties and several hospital websites. Danish municipal IT company Kombit said it had shut down several services, including the national school communication platform. Disruption was even more widespread in Finland, where state IT services provider Valtori said government public network services had been taken offline "as a precautionary measure." France's Interior Ministry said it had placed all of its websites into preventive maintenance.

item.title: Starlink access in Ukraine a decision for Musk, not White House, Rubio says
item.description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that decisions regarding Ukraine's access to Starlink were up to its parent company SpaceX and Elon Musk, not the White House, comments that suggested Musk may have restricted Kyiv's access to the service.
item.dc:creator: Gram Slattery
item.content:encoded: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that decisions regarding Ukraine's access to Starlink were up to its parent company SpaceX and Elon Musk, not the White House, comments that suggested Musk may have restricted Kyiv's access to the service. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that [USN:L6N4661BY TEXT:"Musk had ordered the slowdown"] of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink that Ukraine [USN:L1N4620L4 TEXT:"relies on to defend itself"] against missile attacks from Russia. The Journal cited one person saying that SpaceX CEO Musk, President Donald Trump and White House officials discussed the matter beforehand, and two people saying that Musk and the president discussed the matter in the days after the slowdown. "I'm not aware that we knew about this decision beforehand. But that's irrelevant," Rubio told reporters during a trip to India. "The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they'll allow it to be used at." Musk and SpaceX (SPCX.O) did not respond to requests for comment. Trump, asked by reporters on Wednesday whether Musk ordered the slowdown, said: "I don't know who did it, but I was not involved." Reuters has cited two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter saying [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"the decision ultimately came from the White House"]. This version was also asserted by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, but denied by the administration. Rubio's comments are likely to intensify concerns in Washington regarding Musk's ability to influence US foreign policy. They also represent an apparent shift in position for the administration. Trump has previously said publicly he believed [USN:L6N462112 TEXT:"neither he nor Musk was behind the slowdown"]. Departing for a trip to Uzbekistan and India on Saturday, Rubio had said no one ordered the slowdown, an assertion that drew criticism from lawmakers in both parties. "I'm not sure Zelenskiy knows what he's talking about, but it wasn't deliberate," Rubio said at the time. "We have nothing to do with that. I don't – the United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it's been restored," Rubio said. SENATE DEMOCRATS SEE RISKS TO DELEGATION A Senate Democratic aide said the Starshield slowdown, which occurred during an October 13-16 visit to Kyiv by a bipartisan US congressional delegation, put US lawmakers and staff in the group at risk, along with 230 US personnel on the ground. Russia was now using jet-powered versions of the Shahed drones that could fly at 280 miles per hour (450 km/hour) or faster, which required faster defensive drones to mount an adequate defense, the aide said. "It's a basic math problem. If you have a 280-mph object coming towards you, you are not going to be able to counter it with something that goes 100 mph," the aide said, noting Kyiv had lost a lot of air assets the first night of the slowdown. At the moment, problems with transmission of US data and a slowdown in transmission of security assistance meant that drones were jeopardizing the ability of the staff and delegation members to get to official shelters, the aide said. Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth also portrayed the Starlink cutoff [USN:SPN4650B4 TEXT:"as a commercial matter"]. No US official has publicly said, however, that they have pushed SpaceX to reverse any cutoffs. "There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to, and that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions," Hegseth said. One significant point of confusion relates to the difference between SpaceX's Starshield and Starlink products. Starshield is essentially a military-grade version of Starlink developed for the Pentagon. Rubio suggested on Saturday that Ukraine never had access to Starshield in the first place, while Zelenskiy has said that [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"both Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine have been disrupted"].

item.title: State Bank of India reports cyberattack involving nearly 3,900 customer records
item.description: State Bank of India on Wednesday reported a cyberattack involving 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information that was leaked on the dark web.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: State Bank of India (SBI.NS) on Wednesday reported a cyberattack involving 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information that was leaked on the dark web. The lender said a preliminary analysis showed that the exposed information included customer names, mobile numbers, dates of birth, email addresses, residential addresses, brand and customer identifiers, and loan records. SBI has engaged an independent cybersecurity agency to conduct a comprehensive assessment and investigate the nature and extent of the data leak. "Customer balances are completely safe," the lender said in a post on X. The leak is not expected to have any material impact on the bank's core business operations, financial performance or business continuity, SBI said. The incident comes amid heightened [USN:KCN0YO1FG TEXT:"regulatory focus"], with India's banking regulator pushing lenders to strengthen cybersecurity frameworks in recent years amid a rise in threats targeting financial institutions.

item.title: Stocks rise on AI-led earnings, France's 10-year bond yield hits 5%
item.description: Major stock indexes climbed on Wednesday, lifted by more strong results from AI-focused companies, while France's 10-year bond yield hit 5% for the first time since 2002 due to growing concern about the country's economic outlook.
item.dc:creator: Caroline Valetkevitch, Dhara Ranasinghe
item.content:encoded: Major stock indexes climbed on Wednesday, lifted by more strong results from AI-focused companies, while France's 10-year bond yield hit 5% for the first time since 2002 due to growing concern about the country's economic outlook. The Nasdaq gained more than 1%, with Super Micro (SMCI.O) shares rising 9.5% after the AI server maker forecast quarterly revenue and profit margin above Wall Street estimates. Shares of SpaceX (SPCX.O) [USN:L4N4661M0 TEXT:"shot up"] 7.8% after Elon Musk said late on Tuesday that a merger of his two companies SpaceX and Tesla (TSLA.O) would be "a good idea." SpaceX also posted its first profit as a public company. [USN:L6N45Z12J TEXT:"AI-related shares"] sold off ahead of third-quarter results on investor worries about how long the AI trade can last. item.title: SafePay ransomware group has targeted hundreds this year, US agencies say
item.description: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said on Tuesday that about 600 victims were affected this year by SafePay, one of the world's most active ransomware groups.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said on Tuesday that about 600 victims were affected this year by SafePay, one of the world's most active ransomware groups. Victims range from the Americas to Australia, CISA said in a joint statement with other agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the US Secret Service. SafePay gains network access by accessing compromised credentials and targets "known vulnerabilities" in internet-facing devices, the statement said. The group then steals data and encrypts systems, pressuring victims to pay by threatening to publish the stolen information. In some cases, according to the statement, the group calls victims directly. "SafePay actors have already targeted more than 600 victims worldwide across multiple critical infrastructure sectors," said Brett Leatherman, the assistant director of the FBI's cyber division.

item.title: US Social Security Agency corrects nearly 15% of records in database cleanup
item.description: The US Social Security Administration said on Tuesday that it had corrected records for nearly 15% of all active Social Security numbers, adding missing death and citizenship information, as part of the Trump administration's effort to prevent fraud in the benefits program.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The US Social Security Administration said on Tuesday that it had corrected records for nearly 15% of all active Social Security numbers, adding missing death and citizenship information, as part of the Trump administration's effort to prevent fraud in the benefits program. In what the agency said was the most comprehensive cleanup in its 91-year history, the SSA added 17 million dates of death to records that previously lacked this information It also updated about 25 million records that previously had missing citizenship information using data received from the Department of Homeland Security's Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) service, the SSA said in a statement Combined, those changes mean that nearly 15% of all active SSNs covering about 330 million US citizens and nearly 390 million total records have been corrected, the SSA said, adding that it was working to correct another 8.5 million records with inaccurate citizenship status "Accurate SSN records prevent fraud across federal programs and support the proper administration of benefits," SSA Commissioner Frank Bisignano said in the statement The Social Security Administration administers benefits for tens of millions of older Americans and people with disabilities President Donald Trump vowed to address what he said was fraud and waste in the Social Security system after taking office last year

item.title: What you need to know about the 2026 US midterm elections
item.description: Early voting has been underway for weeks ahead of the November 3, 2026, midterm elections, when US voters will elect members of the House of Representatives and Senate and governors in states across the country.
item.dc:creator: Richard Cowan
item.content:encoded: (This Oct. 19 story has been corrected to say 36 governors, not 39, in paragraph 25.) Early voting has been underway for weeks ahead of the November 3, 2026, midterm elections , when US voters will elect members of the House of Representatives and Senate and governors in states across the country. Held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, the midterms by definition do not involve the president. But for anyone who thinks they lack drama or importance this year, consider these two statistics: More than 100 million people likely will cast ballots in this year's midterm voting, if turnout is anything like the previous midterm in 2022; and as of October 12, a record $3.8 billion had been spent on political advertisements that have been aired so far. Top spending is in battleground US Senate races in Texas, Ohio and Michigan, according to AdImpact, which tracks the activities. [USN:L6N45Y0SX TEXT:"Elon Musk alone"] has spent about $366 million to support Republicans, according to campaign finance records. Still, midterms generally attract fewer voters than the higher-profile presidential races. More than 155 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election, for example. CONTROL OF CONGRESS AT STAKE Plenty is at stake in this midterm election as [USN:L6N45K0S4 TEXT:"Democrats try to win majority control"] of the US Congress. Currently, Republicans hold a 218-214 majority in the House, where there are two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans. Democrats must win a net gain of four seats to win control. Democrats also are fighting to win the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority. They must net four additional seats to get control. Ten races, including those in Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa and Georgia, could decide the outcome. CAN MIDTERMS AFFECT THE PRESIDENCY? Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress. For 2026 that means that President Donald Trump and his Republicans controlling the US Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions. The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, [USN:L1N45V0SB TEXT:"grade the president's performance,"] and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive low marks. Midterm election results also can give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028. WHAT ARE POLLS SHOWING? Approval of [USN:L6N45D0NV TEXT:"Trump's performance"] is at an all-time low of 32%, according to a September Reuters/Ipsos poll. [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"Domestic issues"] like rising consumer prices are likely to have an impact on the outcome of many races and could [USN:L1N45Z0VZ TEXT:"erode support for Republicans."] At the same time, there is evidence that [USN:L4N45T027 TEXT:"Democrats are more enthusiastic"] about voting this year than Republicans. If early voting trends continue it could point to a Democratic win in November. There are also signs that [USN:L6N44B0W4 TEXT:"Latino voters"] who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump's immigration enforcement tactics. However, a landslide for the Democrats is [USN:L1N45N0R3 TEXT:"far from assured"]. Republicans could benefit from continued skepticism towards Democrats, a Republican spending advantage on campaigns, and fears from moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers. RECENT MIDTERM HISTORY Recent history tells the story of the shockwaves a midterm election can produce. In the 2010 midterms, during the Democratic presidency of Barack Obama, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming US economy and weak support for Obama's landmark healthcare reform legislation. Democrats lost their majority. In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats. The Republican wave was [USN:520101108 TEXT:"a "shellacking,""] Obama lamented at the time. He subsequently faced Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defense spending. Democrats [USN:KCN1NC0KY TEXT:"returned the favor"] in 2018, with Trump in the White House. They gained a net total of 40 House seats, but lost a net two Senate seats. This year's elections also have races for governors in 36 of the 50 states and voting in nearly every state for seats in their state-level legislative bodies. Currently, Republicans control 55% of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8%, according to Ballotpedia. WHO WILL BE SPEAKER? If Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker — second in line for the presidency after the vice president — is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York. He is currently the House Democratic leader. Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to [USN:L6N45E0PR TEXT:"launch investigations"] into a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates. Jeffries repeatedly has said Democrats would look into what he has called "unprecedented levels of corruption" during the Trump administration. Jeffries also would steer Democrats' legislative priorities through the House. He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy and other costs more affordable. A Republican win, on the other hand, would ensure that the speaker's gavel remains in that party's hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job. Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defense spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump's 2025 [USN:L1N3T10IT TEXT:""One Big Beautiful Bill.""] MARQUEE RACES Among the most-watched House races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler's bid for reelection to a New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential campaign and an open seat in a Nebraska swing district where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the US war against Iran. Also high on Democrats' list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey. Hovering over all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states. Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted there is widespread cheating in US elections, despite a lack of evidence. State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene.
